issues.legal_issue: A later individual claim to community property cannot displace an operative decree recognizing the community’s right to that property.
material_facts: The community had obtained a decree for possession of the property against a person who claimed a rival title, and that claim had been rejected.
The decree remained operative when the later suit was brought by a person claiming ownership under a separate sale deed and will.
The court could not determine from the available evidence whether the earlier suit had been brought in a representative capacity.
issues.conclusion: The later suit could not succeed while the earlier decree remained operative; the decree dismissing the later suit was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Order I Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes the court’s permission mandatory for a representative suit. However, a community member may sue to assert a right in community property or protect it without satisfying Order I Rule 8, where the suit is not representative. Regardless of the earlier suit’s representative status, its operative decree recognizing the community’s rights made the later suit futile.

predicates.community_property_title_suit: A claimant brings a suit asserting title to property claimed as belonging to a community.
predicates.prior_community_property_decree_still_op: A prior decree recognizing the community’s rights over the property remains operative.

issues.definition: When a suit asserts title to community property and an operative prior decree already recognizes the community’s rights over it, the later suit cannot displace that decree.

issues.legal_issue: A will is not established as genuine merely by evidence of its execution when suspicious circumstances remain unexplained.
material_facts: The will made the claimant the sole legatee while making no provision for the testator’s wife, who was alive when it was executed.
The will was not produced for decades despite opportunities to rely on it in earlier litigation concerning the property.
The evidence concerning the will’s execution and witnesses was unsatisfactory, and the propounder did not satisfactorily explain the suspicious circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The will was not genuine and could not support the claimant’s title.
issues.legal_principle: The propounder must establish a will’s genuineness with trustworthy and unimpeachable evidence. The court may assess not only testimony and demeanour but also circumstances appearing from the evidence or document, surrounding circumstances, and inherent improbabilities. Where suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must remove them to the court’s satisfaction. The court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Devi v. V. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, Smt. Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose, and Mst. Biro v. Atma Ram.

rule.if: will_based_title_claim and surviving_spouse_excluded_without_explanation and will_withheld_despite_opportunities and propounder_failed_to_resolve_suspicion

predicates.will_based_title_claim: A claimant relies on a will to establish title to property.
predicates.surviving_spouse_excluded_without_explan: The will excludes a surviving spouse without an explanation supported by the evidence.
predicates.will_withheld_despite_opportunities: The will was not produced for a lengthy period despite opportunities to rely on it.
predicates.propounder_failed_to_resolve_suspicion: The person propounding the will fails to satisfactorily resolve suspicious circumstances surrounding it.

issues.definition: If a title claim relies on a will that unexplainedly excludes a surviving spouse, was withheld despite opportunities to produce it, and is surrounded by suspicion the propounder fails to resolve, the will is not established as genuine.

issues.legal_issue: An ordinary copy of a document whose original is unavailable is not admissible as secondary evidence unless its correctness is proved by proper evidence.
material_facts: The claimant relied on an old sale deed as the foundation of title but did not produce the original or a certified copy.
The copy produced was an ordinary copy, without an endorsement establishing it as a true copy or evidence showing that it had been compared with the original.
The witness who produced it had no personal knowledge of its registration and did not produce the register; no evidence established the contents of the original.
issues.conclusion: The ordinary copy was not secondary evidence and could not support the claimant’s title.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 63 and 79 of the Indian Evidence Act govern the kinds of secondary evidence and the presumption as to the correctness of certified copies. Correctness is presumed for certified copies within Section 63(1), but other copies must be proved by proper evidence. A certified copy of a registered sale deed may be produced as secondary evidence when the original is unavailable; an unverified ordinary copy is not thereby admissible.

rule.if: title_suit_based_on_document and original_unavailable and copy_not_certified and copy_correctness_unproved

predicates.title_suit_based_on_document: A claimant brings a title suit relying on a document as the foundation of title.
predicates.original_unavailable: The original document is not produced.
predicates.copy_not_certified: The copy produced is not certified as a true copy.
predicates.copy_correctness_unproved: No proper evidence establishes that the copy is correct or establishes the contents of the original.

issues.definition: In a title suit relying on a document, when the original is unavailable and the claimant produces an uncertified copy whose correctness is not proved, that copy is not admissible as secondary evidence.
